entities.name: Tufayl ibn Amr
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Al-Ṭufayl ibn ʿAmr al-Dawsī, a pre-eminent chieftain of the Banu Daws tribe from the Tihama region of ancient Arabia, emerged as a pivotal figure in the nascent Islamic community during the early 7th century CE. Renowned for his poetic eloquence, sagacity, and tribal leadership, Tufayl's conversion to Islam around 619 CE marked a significant turning point, not only for his powerful tribe but also for the burgeoning Muslim movement seeking adherents beyond Mecca. His early embrace of the new faith, prior to the Hijra, positioned him as one of the distinguished Sahaba (Companions of the Prophet Muhammad) and a key proponent of its message in the remote, mountainous territories of his people.

Upon encountering the Prophet Muhammad in Mecca, Tufayl, initially wary due to Meccan warnings, famously listened to the Quran and embraced Islam. He then returned to his tribe, the Banu Daws, in Tihama, where he embarked on an intensive mission of dawah (inviting others to Islam). Despite initial resistance, his persistent efforts, including a miraculous light that emanated from his forehead (or staff), led to the gradual conversion of his entire tribe. He subsequently led a contingent of 400 Dawsī families to Medina, joining the Prophet Muhammad after the Battle of Khaybar in 628 CE, bolstering the Muslim forces and demonstrating the faith's growing appeal among influential Arabian tribes.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Tufayl ibn Amr's early conversion and successful propagation of Islam among his powerful Banu Daws tribe significantly expanded the Muslim community. His subsequent leadership in the Ridda Wars was crucial for the consolidation of the nascent Islamic state under Abu Bakr, impacting the future political and religious landscape of the Arabian Peninsula.
